title: The Change Request: From Ticket to CAB

blocks.text: In security, an uncontrolled change is an outage waiting to happen. Objective **1.2** measures your ability to explain how a change management process reduces risk: **who requests, who approves, what impacts are analyzed, and how we roll back**.
Change as a Cause of Incidents

The SOC notes devote two pages to the **change request** and the **CAB**: a change can be technical (patch, configuration, application) or organizational (process, role), but in all cases it must be **requested, evaluated, approved, scheduled, tested, and documented**. It is this traceability that the exam seeks to verify, not mastery of a ticketing tool.

blocks.note: Change request and Change Advisory Board (pp. 135-136)

blocks.field: Group of stakeholders (IT, security, business, operations) that reviews change requests, evaluates their impact, and grants or denies approval before production deployment.

items: **Requester / owner**: the person who submits the request and remains responsible until closure.
**CAB**: arbitrates risk and schedule, especially for high-impact changes.
**Stakeholders**: business, support, security, vendors — they experience or validate the effect of the change.
**Change manager**: prepares the file, checks completeness, and archives decisions.

items.title: 1. Opening the Ticket
items.text: Describe the change, its reason, the affected system, the owner, and stakeholders (SOCN pp. 38-40).

items.title: 2. Impact Analysis
items.text: Identify affected services, dependencies, users, and security controls.

items.title: 3. CAB Review and Approval
items.text: The board decides: approved, rejected, or approved with conditions (window, additional testing).

items.title: 4. Maintenance Window Scheduling
items.text: Choose a low-impact slot, announce expected downtime, and notify business units.

items.title: 5. Testing and Results
items.text: Validate in a test environment, record results, then apply in production.

items.title: 6. Backout and Closure
items.text: Keep an executable rollback plan ready until the end of the window, then document.

blocks.text: **Impact analysis** must cover three dimensions: availability (downtime, restart), security (allow list changes, port openings), and continuity (dependencies, legacy applications). A "harmless" change on one server can break an entire dependency chain.

blocks.note: Prioritization and impact of operations on SOC availability (printed pp. 35-36)

left.title: Backout Planning
points: **Return to the previous state** if the change fails.
Requires a backup, a known configuration, and a tested procedure.
Typical answer when a scenario mentions an immediate outage after deployment.

right.title: Fail Forward
points: **Move forward** with a patch, workaround, or new version rather than rolling back.
Chosen when rollback is impossible or riskier (data already migrated).
Must remain an explicit, documented decision, not improvisation.

blocks.text: Classic trap: presenting **rollback** as an automatic solution. A backout is only reliable if it has been **tested** and if the maintenance window leaves enough time to execute it.

blocks.q: A patch is applied in production. Ten minutes later, authentications fail. Which action is expected first?
options: Open a new change request for next month
Execute the backout plan within the maintenance window, then document the failure
Wait until the end of the window to notify the CAB
blocks.explain: The backout plan exists precisely for this case: it must be executable during the window, then the failure is recorded and re-analyzed by the CAB.

items: A change is requested, evaluated, approved, scheduled, tested, applied, and documented.
The CAB arbitrates; the owner bears responsibility; stakeholders experience the impact.
Backout = return to previous state; fail forward = move forward with a fix.

blocks.text: A change is not judged solely on its technical success: it must also **leave the environment in a documented, consistent, and secure state**. This is the part most often forgotten in exam scenarios.
Allow Lists, Restricted Activities, and Restarts

blocks.field: Control mechanism that explicitly permits or blocks addresses, applications, or commands. A change can modify these lists: the security effect must be analyzed before application.

items: **Allow lists / deny lists**: verify that a new rule does not open a prohibited flow (e.g., adding an IP range to an allow list).
**Restricted activities**: certain actions require heightened authorization (administrator access, production, maintenance).
**Downtime**: announced and accepted unavailability duration during the window.
**Service restart / application restart**: a restart can reset sessions, certificates, or processing queues.
**Legacy applications**: an unsupported application may be the only system depending on an old protocol or port.
**Dependencies**: database, directory, DNS, certificates, API — recovery depends on the slowest link.

blocks.note: Rollback, restoration, and system dependencies (printed p. 104)

blocks.text: If a scenario mentions a legacy application that "must absolutely remain available", look for the hidden **dependency** (port, service, service account) in the expected answer.

A change that modifies a security control (firewall, MFA, logging, encryption) must be reviewed by security **before** the CAB: that is often where regressions hide. The **Defensive Security Handbook** emphasizes the need to document decisions and keep procedures up to date after every intervention.

blocks.note: Documentation, standards, and procedures kept up to date (printed p. 144)

head: Item to Update
Why
rows: An outdated diagram makes the next impact analysis wrong.
The procedure must reflect the configuration actually deployed.
Identifying the exact version in production enables rollback and auditing.

blocks.note: Version control and change tracking (printed p. 172)
Patch management and version tracking (printed p. 175)
SOPs / runbooks and repeatable execution of operations (printed pp. 130-132)

blocks.text: **Version control** is not limited to code: it also covers configurations, deployment scripts, and policies. Without it, backout relies on an administrator's memory.

blocks.q: After a successful change, which updates are part of closure?
options: Only the ticket; the rest will be done at the next audit
Only the application version in the inventory
None: the CAB handles it automatically
blocks.explain: Post-change documentation is an explicit requirement: diagrams, policies/procedures, and version control must reflect the actual state.

items: Analyze the change's effect on allow/deny lists, restarts, downtime, and dependencies.
Legacy applications and security controls deserve special attention.
Closure = diagrams + policies/procedures + up-to-date version control.
An untested or undocumented backout is not a reliable plan.
